title: Christmas Day
hook: many Orthodox keep Christmas on 7 January by the old calendar

segments.voice: Yesterday, Christmas Eve: shepherds awake in a dark field, and candles passed down the rows. Your line was silent night, holy night. Did you give the dark a minute of stillness? Day one thousand eleven.

Two families, one faith, and two different Christmas mornings. In one house, the feast is today, in December, with the tree and the big meal. In another, the decorations are still waiting, because their church keeps Christmas in January. Some Orthodox churches still count the year by the older Julian calendar, which has drifted out of step with the calendar on your phone. So their Christmas lands in what everyday calendars call January. Same feast. Same story. Same child. Just a different page of the calendar. And whichever morning it is, the churches gather around one word for what happened. Today, the Nativity.

Nativity is an old word for a birth, and the Christian calendar uses it for other births too, but on its own it means this one. Luke tells it in a single plain sentence. In the King James Bible: "And she brought forth her firstborn son, and wrapped him in swaddling clothes, and laid him in a manger; because there was no room for them in the inn." That's it. No description of the baby, no speeches. A manger is an animal's feeding trough. Whatever else was happening, the child's first bed was where the animals ate. Churches hear another text alongside it, from the prophet Isaiah: "For unto us a child is born, unto us a son is given: and the government shall be upon his shoulder." Read on Christmas, it sounds like a birth announcement. Christians hear it as fulfilled in Jesus; in Jewish reading, Isaiah is speaking about a king of his own day, and the book was theirs first. Notice the little word us. Not unto the world. Not unto the righteous. Unto us. Read aloud in church on Christmas morning, it sounds as if whoever is listening is being handed the child. Catholic, Orthodox and Protestant churches keep the Nativity, each in its own way. Orthodox icons of the feast show the baby in a dark cave, wrapped so tightly some readers see burial bands, as if the end of the story is already folded into the beginning. Western churches often set up a crib scene, with ox and donkey, shepherds, and later the magi. And underneath every version is the claim Christians build the feast on: that God came near as a newborn, small enough to be laid in a feeding trough.
screen: `A CAVE, A CRIB, A FEEDING TROUGH.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: decide who you'll wish a blessed Christmas today. Settle, and breathe. Let faces come: family, a neighbor, someone working today while others rest, someone spending the day alone. Choose one person who might not hear it from anyone else. Think about how you'll say it: a call, a message, a word at the door. Keep it simple. If you pray, you can hold that person before God, with the line from Isaiah: unto us a child is born. If you don't, simply hold them in mind and plan the words. The bell holds the time.
Nativity. An old word for a birth, and the Christian name for Christmas: the child wrapped and laid in a manger, because there was no room in the inn.
Your line: unto us a child. Today, send the person you chose a blessed Christmas, and mean the us in it. Day one thousand eleven.

howItsDone: Christians celebrate the Nativity with services on Christmas Eve or Christmas morning, carols, crib scenes and shared meals; some Orthodox churches keep the feast in January because they follow the older Julian calendar.
